---
title: "The Podium Edge"
subtitle: "Do taller and heavier swimmers have a competitive advantage at the Olympics?"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

```{r}
#| label: podium-comparison
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

library(tidyverse)

df <- read_csv("data/olympics.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(sport == "Swimming", year >= 1980, !is.na(height), !is.na(weight)) |>
  mutate(
    status = if_else(!is.na(medal), "Medalist", "Non-Medalist"),
    sex = if_else(sex == "M", "Men", "Women")
  )

ggplot(df, aes(x = height, fill = status)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.55) +
  facet_wrap(~sex, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    title = "Olympic Swimming Medalists Are Significantly Taller",
    subtitle = "Height distributions of medalists vs. non-medalists (1980–2016)",
    x = "Height (cm)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## The Height Advantage in Elite Swimming

Reaching the Olympic Games requires extraordinary conditioning, but reaching the podium correlates strongly with physical size:

- **Men**: The median male medalist stands at **190 cm** (6'3") and weighs **84 kg**, compared to a median of **185 cm** and **79 kg** for non-medalist competitors.
- **Women**: The median female medalist stands at **175 cm** (5'9") and weighs **65 kg**, compared to **172 cm** and **62 kg** among non-medalists.

Greater stature provides longer lever arms for propulsion and allows swimmers to reach further on turns and finishes, creating a measurable separation at the highest level of competition.
